title: The Gospel Canticles: Magnificat, Benedictus, Nunc Dimittis
lead: The songs in Luke's birth stories, sung by Mary (Luke 1:46–55), Zechariah (Luke 1:68–79) and Simeon (Luke 2:29–32), with the angels' short "Glory to God" (Luke 2:14). They are woven from Israel's psalms and songs, Hannah's above all, and they became daily songs of Christian worship.

sections.b: Almost every line of the three songs echoes the Greek Old Testament. Mary's song follows Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1–10): a woman given a child praises the God who brings down the mighty and lifts the poor (1 Samuel 2:7–8; Psalm 113:7–8). Zechariah's song is built on the promises to David and Abraham (Psalm 132:17; Genesis 22:16–17; Micah 7:20) and ends with light for those in darkness (Isaiah 9:2). Simeon's song draws on Isaiah's servant songs: salvation seen by every people and a light to the nations (Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 52:10). Israel's earlier songs of rescue, Miriam's, Deborah's and Judith's, stand behind them (Exodus 15:1–21; Judges 5; Judith 16).
sections.refs: Luke 1:46–55; Luke 1:68–79; Luke 2:29–32; 1 Samuel 2:1–10; Psalm 113:7–8; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 9:2

sections.b: Readers have long noticed that the songs fit their singers only loosely: Mary sings of "Israel" and of rulers pulled down, more like a victory hymn than a private prayer. Views: (1) the singers spoke them, perhaps in Hebrew or Aramaic, and Luke preserved them; (2) Luke composed them in the style of the Greek Old Testament, as ancient historians composed speeches; (3) Luke used earlier hymns of Jewish Christians, perhaps from the circle Raymond Brown called the Anawim, "the poor ones"; (4) Paul Winter and others suggested Jewish hymns from the Maccabean wars, adapted. Most scholars hold some form of (2) or (3), and most hear a Semitic style beneath the Greek.

In the Western church the Benedictus is sung at Lauds (morning prayer), the Magnificat at Vespers (evening prayer) and the Nunc Dimittis at Compline (night prayer). The Anglican Book of Common Prayer kept the Magnificat and Nunc Dimittis at Evening Prayer, and composers from Tallis to the present have set them. In Orthodox Matins the Magnificat is sung with the refrain "More honorable than the cherubim." The angels' song (Luke 2:14) opens the Gloria of the Mass and of the Orthodox Great Doxology. Luther wrote a whole commentary on the Magnificat (1521) for a young prince, as a lesson in how God treats the lowly and the proud.
